record.paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: Attribution-based explanations and counterfactual recourse should ideally be robust, meaning small input changes do not cause large explanation jumps, and recourse-sensitive, meaning following the explanation direction can achieve sufficient utility. What practical workarounds can overcome or manage the impossibility of satisfying both properties simultaneously?

evidence.quote: Two desirable properties of explanation methods are robustness and recourse sensitivity [162].
Fokkema et al. [162] point out that attribution methods and counterfactual explanations cannot be robust and recourse sensitive at the same time.
Future work should therefore consider workarounds to circumvent Fokkema et al. [162]’s impossibility result.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a predictor on an input space $\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ (interpreted, e.g., as the score of a binary classifier with decision threshold $\tau$). An attribution-based explanation method is a map $E:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ that assigns to each input $x$ a vector of feature weights $E(x)=(E_1(x),\dots,E_d(x))$. A counterfactual explanation method is a map $C:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}$ producing for each $x$ a perturbation $\delta(x)=C(x)-x$ (which can be reinterpreted as an attribution).

Two desiderata are formulated for such an explanation method $E$ with respect to $f$:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Robustness}: $E$ is continuous (or Lipschitz) in $x$; i.e., for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\|x-x'\|<\delta$ implies $\|E(x)-E(x')\|<\varepsilon$.
\item \emph{Recourse sensitivity}: for every $x$ with $f(x)<\tau$ that admits a feasible recourse, moving from $x$ in the direction indicated by $E(x)$ by a bounded step size yields an input $x'$ with $f(x')\ge\tau$ (i.e., following the explanation achieves sufficient utility).
\end{itemize}

It is known that for broad classes of predictors $f$, no single-valued attribution method $E$ can simultaneously be robust and recourse-sensitive: any $E$ satisfying recourse sensitivity must be discontinuous, and any continuous $E$ must fail recourse sensitivity on some inputs. The same impossibility extends to counterfactual explanation maps $C$.

Problem. Develop and rigorously analyze practical workarounds that circumvent this impossibility. Concretely, formulate relaxations or alternative formats for explanation methods—such as (i) set-valued attribution maps $E:\mathcal{X}\to 2^{\mathbb{R}^d}$ that return multiple admissible explanations per input, (ii) probabilistic or distribution-valued explanation methods, (iii) explanations defined only on restricted regions of $\mathcal{X}$ where $f$ satisfies regularity assumptions, or (iv) approximate versions of robustness and recourse sensitivity with quantitative trade-off bounds—and identify sufficient conditions on $f$ and on the explanation format under which both robustness (suitably relaxed) and recourse sensitivity (suitably relaxed) can be guaranteed simultaneously. Characterize the achievable Pareto frontier between the two properties.
artifact.status_search_result: The underlying impossibility theorem (attribution-based explanations cannot be both robust and recourse-sensitive) was established by Fokkema, de Heide, and van Erven (arXiv:2205.15834; JMLR 2023). That work suggests partial workarounds, such as set-valued attribution outputs, and gives sufficient conditions for recourse sensitivity in restricted function classes, but a general, fully satisfactory practical resolution of the trade-off is not established and remains an active research direction.

status_evidence.title: Attribution-based Explanations that Provide Recourse Cannot be Robust
status_evidence.snippet: Proves no single attribution method can be both recourse-sensitive and robust; discusses workarounds like set-valued outputs and sufficient conditions for some function classes.
status_evidence.claim: Establishes the impossibility result and proposes partial workarounds, leaving a general resolution open.

status_evidence.title: Attribution-based Explanations that Provide Recourse Cannot be Robust (JMLR)
status_evidence.snippet: Published version of the impossibility theorem covering LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad, and counterfactual explanations.
status_evidence.claim: Confirms the impossibility result is formally established; general practical workarounds remain open.

status_evidence.title: Impossibility Theorems for Feature Attribution
status_evidence.snippet: Related impossibility results for attribution methods.
status_evidence.claim: Indicates ongoing research into limitations of feature attribution methods.
